paragraphs: Ippolit Kirillovitch had picked the historical method of telling his story. Nervous speakers love it, because its fixed limits keep their own eager rhetoric in check. At this point he turned aside into a long discussion of Grushenka’s “first lover,” and put forward several interesting thoughts on the subject.

“Karamazov had been frantically jealous of everyone. Yet before this first lover he simply collapsed and effaced himself on the spot. That makes it stranger still, since he seems to have given this formidable rival hardly a thought. He saw him as a danger far away, and Karamazov always lives in the present. Perhaps he took him for a fiction. But his wounded heart saw at once that the woman had been hiding this new rival from him and deceiving him. The man was anything but a fiction to her. He was the one hope of her life. The moment Karamazov grasped this, he gave in.

“Gentlemen of the jury, I cannot help dwelling on this unexpected side of the prisoner’s character. Suddenly he shows an irresistible longing for justice, a respect for woman, an acknowledgment of her right to love. And this at the very moment when he had stained his hands with his father’s blood for her sake! True, the blood he had shed was already crying out for vengeance. He had ruined his soul and his life in this world, and in that same instant he had to ask himself what he was now, and what he could be, to her, the being dearer to him than his own soul. He had to measure himself against that former lover, who had come back repentant, with a new love, to the woman he once betrayed, with honorable offers and the promise of a reformed and happy life. And what could he, the luckless man, give her now? What could he offer her?

“Karamazov felt all this. He knew that his crime had closed every road to him, and that he was a criminal under sentence, not a man with a life ahead of him! The thought crushed him. So he flew at once to one frantic plan, which a man of Karamazov’s character must have seen as the only possible escape from his terrible position. That escape was suicide. He ran to get the pistols he had left in pledge with his friend Perhotin. And as he ran, he pulled out of his pocket the money he had stained his hands with his father’s gore to get. Oh, now he needed money more than ever. Karamazov would die, Karamazov would shoot himself, and people would remember it! He was a poet, after all, and he had burned the candle at both ends all his life. ‘To her, to her! And there, oh, there I will throw a feast for the whole world, the like of which was never seen, and people will remember it and talk of it for years! Amid shouts of wild merriment, reckless gypsy songs and dances, I will raise my glass and drink to the woman I adore and to her new happiness! And then and there, at her feet, I will blow my brains out before her and punish myself! She will think of Mitya Karamazov now and then. She will see how Mitya loved her. She will feel for Mitya!’

“Here we see, in excess, the love of effect, the romantic despair and sentimentality, and the wild recklessness of the Karamazovs. Yes, but there is something more, gentlemen of the jury, something that cries out in the soul, throbs without rest in the mind, and poisons the heart unto death. That _something_ is conscience, gentlemen of the jury, its verdict, its terrible torments! The pistol will settle everything, the pistol is the only way out! But _beyond_—I do not know whether Karamazov, at that moment, asked himself ‘What lies beyond?’ or whether a Karamazov could, like Hamlet, ask ‘What lies beyond?’ No, gentlemen of the jury, other nations have their Hamlets, but we still have our Karamazovs!”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch gave a minute account of Mitya’s preparations: the scene at Perhotin’s, at the shop, with the drivers. He cited many words and actions, all backed up by witnesses, and the picture made a terrible impression on the audience. Once the facts were set side by side, the guilt of this harassed, desperate man stood out clear and convincing.

“What need had he to be careful? Two or three times he came close to confessing. He hinted at it, he all but said it outright.” (Then came the witnesses’ evidence.) “He even shouted to the peasant who was driving him, ‘Do you know you are driving a murderer?’ But he could not speak out. He had to reach Mokroe and finish his romance there. And what was waiting for the luckless man? Almost from the first minute at Mokroe he saw that his unbeatable rival might not be so unbeatable after all, and that the toast to their new happiness was neither wanted nor welcome. But you know the facts, gentlemen of the jury, from the preliminary inquiry. Karamazov’s triumph over his rival was complete, and his soul entered a wholly new phase, perhaps the most terrible one it has passed through or ever will.

“One may say with certainty, gentlemen of the jury,” the prosecutor went on, “that outraged nature and the criminal heart exact their own vengeance more fully than any earthly justice. More than that: justice and punishment on earth actually lighten the punishment of nature. At such moments they are even necessary to the criminal’s soul, to save it from despair. For I cannot picture the horror and the moral agony of Karamazov when he learned that she loved him, that for his sake she had turned away her first lover, that she was calling him, Mitya, to a new life and promising him happiness. And when was this? When everything was finished for him and nothing was possible!

“Let me note in passing, in parentheses, a point of importance for the light it throws on the prisoner’s position at that moment. This woman, this love of his, had remained until the last moment, until the very instant of his arrest, a being out of reach, passionately desired by him yet out of reach. Why, then, did he not shoot himself at that time? Why did he drop his plan and even forget where his pistol was? It was exactly that passionate longing for love, and the hope of satisfying it, that held him back. Through all their revels he stayed close to his adored mistress, who sat with him at the banquet and who was more charming and fascinating to him than ever. He did not leave her side, abasing himself before her in his homage.

“His passion might well stifle, for a moment, not only the fear of arrest but even the torments of conscience. For a moment, oh, only for a moment! I can picture the state of mind of a criminal hopelessly enslaved by such influences. First, the influence of drink, of noise and excitement, of the thud of the dance and the scream of the song, and of her, flushed with wine, singing and dancing and laughing to him! Second, the hope, in the background, that the fatal end might still be far off, that at least until morning they would not come to take him. So he had a few hours, and that is much, very much! In a few hours a man can think of many things. I imagine he felt something like what criminals feel on the way to the scaffold. They have another long, long street ahead of them, to be traveled at a walking pace, past thousands of people. Then comes a turn into another street, and only at the end of that street, the dreaded place of execution! At the start of the journey, I imagine, the condemned man, sitting on his shameful cart, must feel that he still has infinite life before him. The houses fall behind, the cart rolls on. Oh, that is nothing, the turn into the second street is still far off, and he still looks boldly to right and left at those thousands of callously curious people with their eyes on him, and still imagines that he is just a man like them. But now the turn comes, into the next street. Oh, that is nothing, nothing, there is still a whole street before him, and however many houses have gone by, he will still think many are left. And so to the very end, to the very scaffold.

“This, I imagine, is how it was with Karamazov then. ‘They have not had time yet,’ he must have thought. ‘I may still find a way out. Oh, there is still time to work out some plan of defense, and now, now—she is so fascinating!’

“His soul was full of confusion and dread, yet he managed to set aside half his money and hide it somewhere. I can explain in no other way why fully half of the three thousand he had just taken from his father’s pillow has vanished. He had been in Mokroe more than once. He had already caroused there for two days running, and he knew the big old house with all its passages and outbuildings. I imagine that part of the money was hidden in that house, not long before the arrest, in some crevice, under some floorboard, in some corner, under the roof. For what purpose? I shall be asked. Why, the catastrophe might strike at any moment, of course. He had not yet thought how to meet it, he had no time, his head was throbbing and his heart was with _her_. But money, money was needed in any case! With money a man is always a man. Perhaps such foresight at such a moment strikes you as unnatural? But he tells us himself that a month earlier, at a critical and exciting moment, he had divided his money in half and sewn it into a little bag. That was not true, as we shall shortly prove. But it shows that the idea was a familiar one to Karamazov, that he had turned it over in his mind. And there is more. When he declared at the inquiry that he had put fifteen hundred roubles in a bag (which never existed), he may have invented that bag on the inspiration of the moment. For two hours earlier he had divided his money and hidden half of it at Mokroe until morning, against an emergency, simply to avoid carrying it on him. Two extremes, gentlemen of the jury. Remember that Karamazov can entertain two extremes, and both at once.

“We have searched the house, but we have not found the money. It may still be there. Or it may have vanished the next day and be in the prisoner’s hands now. In any case, he was at her side, on his knees before her. She was lying on the bed, he had his hands stretched out to her, and he had forgotten everything so completely that he did not even hear the men come to arrest him. He had no time to prepare a line of defense in his mind. He was taken by surprise and confronted with his judges, the arbiters of his fate.

“Gentlemen of the jury, there are moments in the discharge of our duties when it is terrible for us to face a man, terrible for his sake, too! I mean the moments of watching that animal fear, when the criminal sees that all is lost, yet still struggles, still means to struggle. Every instinct of self-preservation rises in him at once. He looks at you with questioning, suffering eyes. He studies you, your face, your thoughts, unsure on which side you will strike. His distracted mind forms thousands of plans in an instant, but he is still afraid to speak, afraid of giving himself away! This purgatory of the spirit, this animal thirst for self-preservation, these humiliating moments of the human soul are awful. Sometimes they stir horror and pity for the criminal even in the lawyer. And that is what we all witnessed then.

“At first he was thunderstruck, and in his terror he let fall some very damaging phrases. ‘Blood! I deserve it!’ But he quickly pulled himself together. He had not prepared what to say or what answer to give. He had nothing ready but a bare denial: ‘I am not guilty of my father’s death.’ That was his fence for the moment, and behind it he hoped to throw up some kind of barricade. He hurried to explain away his first damaging cries by declaring that he was responsible only for the death of the servant Grigory. ‘Of that bloodshed I am guilty, but who killed my father, gentlemen, who killed him? Who can have killed him, _if not I_?’ Do you hear? He asked us that, us, who had come to put that very question to him! Do you hear that phrase, blurted out in such premature haste—‘if not I’? The animal cunning of it, the naïveté, the Karamazov impatience! ‘I did not kill him, and you must not think I did! I wanted to kill him, gentlemen, I wanted to kill him,’ he hurries to admit (he was in a hurry, in a terrible hurry), ‘but still I am not guilty, it was not I who murdered him.’ He grants us that he wanted to murder him, as though to say: you see for yourselves how truthful I am, so you will believe all the sooner that I did not murder him. Oh, in such cases the criminal is often amazingly shallow and credulous.

“At that point one of the lawyers asked him, as if by chance, the simplest of questions: ‘Wasn’t it Smerdyakov who killed him?’ Then, just as we expected, he was horribly angry that we had got ahead of him and caught him off guard, before he had time to prepare the ground and pick the moment when it would be most natural to bring in Smerdyakov’s name. He rushed at once to the opposite extreme, as he always does, and began assuring us that Smerdyakov could not have killed him, was not capable of it. But do not believe him. That was only cunning. He did not really give up the idea of Smerdyakov. On the contrary, he meant to bring him forward again, for indeed he had no one else to bring forward. But he would do it later, because for the moment that line was spoiled for him. He would bring him forward perhaps the next day, or even a few days later, choosing his chance to cry out to us, ‘You know I doubted Smerdyakov’s guilt more than you did, you remember that yourselves, but now I am convinced. He killed him, he must have done!’ For now, meanwhile, he falls back on a gloomy, irritable denial. Impatience and anger drove him, however, into the most clumsy and incredible account of how he looked in at his father’s window and how he respectfully withdrew. The worst of it was that he did not know how matters stood, or what evidence Grigory had given.
